blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GRIFFITHS

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR SIMON WOOD (read)
Members of the jury, the first such statement is made by a Simon Wood, dated 1 April 2019.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Mr Wood states his qualifications and professional experience and leads up to stating:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I was appointed full time in 2003 as a consultant obstetricianal gynaecologist with an interest in fertility at the Countess of Chester Hospital. In 2017 I ceased practising obstetrics to concentrate purely on fertility and to run the IVF service here [that's the Countess].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "This statement relates to a baby called [Baby E].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby E] was born on 29 July 2015 and passed away on 4 August 2015. He was one of a set of twins. The other twin is a boy called [Baby F]. [Baby E]'s mother is called [Mother of Babies E & F].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby E]'s gestation period at delivery was 29 weeks and 5 days. I have viewed [Baby E]'s medical notes prior to completing this statement.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby E]'s case is slightly unusual as it appears to be an in utero transfer from the Liverpool Women's Hospital. His mother, [Mother of Babies E & F], had no antenatal care within the Countess of Chester Hospital as she was booked for delivery at the Liverpool Women's Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Her first contact with the Countess was following an arrangement for transfer to and delivery at the Countess of Chester Hospital. Delivery was required because of absent and reverse end-diastolic flow through the umbilical cord in twin 1. It was decided that the Countess of Chester Hospital was the nearest unit to the Liverpool Women's that had capacity to care for twins of that gestation.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies E & F] arrived at the Countess at 13.55 on 29 July 2015. It is documented by the admitting midwife, by the name of Williams, that she was transferred by ambulance from Liverpool with magnesium sulphate running at that point.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On arrival at the Countess of Chester, [Mother of Babies E & F] was assessed by the ST2 trainee, Dr Harden(?). She had been given steroids on a number of days in the preceding period, that is to say the 22nd and 23rd, and then again on the 26th and 27th, and she was on magnesium sulphate, which commenced at 10.40 hours. Magnesium sulphate is initiated in preterm infants as there is evidence that it is neuroprotective.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Dr Ward and Dr Rowe had discussions with each other, both with the patient and with the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: With regard to the timing of the delivery, it would appear that they wanted the magnesium sulphate to be fully run through, which gave a time of delivery at some time after 5 o'clock in the afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I would have been on call that day and, from looking at the notes and also discussions I have had with Dr Rowe, Dr Rowe was the obstetrician of the week that week, who was covering the delivery suite between 08.30 and completion of the handover to the on-call consultant from 17.00 to 17.30 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "We have a system where one consultant is on 8 until 5 or 8.30 until 5 and covering everything during the hot week but does not do their on-calls that week, and each consultant has their own set of on-calls.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Mother of Babies E & F] was taken into theatre at 17.20 for a spinal anaesthesia to be sited by the anaesthetist.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: When the anaesthetist was happy that the spinal anaesthetic was effective, I then undertook the caesarean section on [Mother of Babies E & F] along with Dr Whitton(?) who was assisting me. Also documented as present was a midwife, Adam, and a scrub nurse, Netherton.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "There were also neonatal staff present in order to take care of the babies once they were born. There would be at least one, if not two, neonatal nurses, as is the policy for a set of twins. There will have also certainly been a registrar present and the senior house officer because they usually have one (inaudible) each.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Referring to the electronic case notes recorded at the time of delivery, surgery would have started at around 17.51, the first twin was delivered at 17.53, and the second twin at 17.54. There was nothing exceptional about the caesarean section. It was a completely and utterly routine caesarean section.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The twins were born in good condition with Apgar scores of 9 at 5 [minutes] and 8 at 5 [minutes]. They seemed well. The blood gases were good. We always check that the gases are normal to ensure no evidence of intrauterine hypoxia. The babies were well oxygenated with no issues and were breathing fine. They then went to the neonatal unit. That was the last involvement with the twins and their mother that I had.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby E] passed away in the early hours of 4 August 2015, 5 days after he was delivered. I would not have been made aware of
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: this. There would have been a review of [Baby E]'s death and we get to see it in the perinatal mortality meetings. They were held roughly once a month, now two-monthly.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "All stillbirths, neonatal deaths and significant morbidity are reviewed by the lead clinicians for obstetrics and paediatrics and presented to the obstetric and paediatric department jointly at the perinatal mortality/morbidity meeting.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Present at these meetings is a paediatric pathologist from Alder Hey who will present post-mortem findings or, if not available, then placental histology so that causes of death can be identified if possible and plans put in place for future pregnancies."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I read documentation in the notes from Sue Brookes, who is a midwife, which stated that the neonatal unit had rung through for [Baby E]'s mother to come down and see him within half an hour. blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I always remember Sue saying during handover, 'I can't believe they said half an hour, she just wanted to go down'.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Sue has documented she took mum down to see [Baby E] following this conversation. Sue didn't document who it was she spoke to. This piece of documentation is how I remember the case.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "There were no factors in [Baby E]'s delivery which gave any cause for concern apart from the fact that he was born prematurely, namely 29 weeks. They are, by definition, very small at that age and would potentially be immediately assisted with their breathing to do this.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't see anything in the notes to indicate whether [Baby E] required any assistance. The care of babies in theatre is more under the doctors, I would say, than the midwives.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Once a baby is delivered, they are passed over to the midwife to then take on to the resus with the doctors. Ultimately, the care normally falls under the paediatricians in theatre. Summary of interview with LUCY LETBY re [Baby F] (read)

My Lord, the final piece of evidence, subject to any minor additions at a later stage, concerns the interview. So this, of course, as you understand, you know the drill, ladies and gentlemen, it's very much a summary.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When she was interviewed on 10 June 2019, Lucy Letby remembered [Baby F] as the surviving twin of [Baby E].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She recalled [Baby E] as he had died and that had affected her.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She didn't remember the incident other than looking at the notes that were provided to her. She agreed that it was her signature alongside the TPN bag entry at 00.25 hours on 5 August 2015, but she could not remember whether she had administered the TPN bag or not. She identified the other signatory as [Nurse A].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that TPN bags were kept in the locked fridge at the bottom of the fridge and the insulin was kept at the top of the fridge. She said all nurses, including nursery nurses, had access to the fridge along with the doctors.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said there was one set of keys that would be passed between them and that the pharmacist also had access to the fridge. She said that the relevant TPN bag would have been made up in the pharmacy and labelled "Twin 2 [Surname of Babies E & F]" in a secure bag.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It would have been marked up to this effect as this would have been checked before being set up. She was unsure whether TPN bags had a port for the addition of medication, but in any event medication would not be added to a TPN bag.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that if a bag had to be disconnected, it should not be reattached as it would no longer be sterile. She said if the bag had been taken off, the only circumstances in which she would reattach it would be if she could definitely guarantee that the end had been kept sterile.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that if a bag had to be removed, it could be replaced with a standard bag, a handful of which were kept as stock in the fridge at all times. They were not prescribed and didn't have specific children's names on them and were just generic bags that any baby could use.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that once a bag was disconnected, it would be disposed of in the sluice room.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby agreed that there was a significant drop in [Baby F]'s blood sugar in the reading at 01.54 hours on 5 August. She said this was dangerously low. She had no idea what had happened to cause the dramatic decline that followed and she denied deliberately harming [Baby F] and denied injecting him with insulin.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When she was interviewed on 12 June 2019, Lucy Letby was asked whether she had placed insulin in [Baby F]'s TPN bag. She denied this. Lucy Letby asked the police whether [Baby F]'s TPN bag was checked and asked the officers how they knew after the event whether the insulin was there at the time the bag was checked.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It was pointed out that she had conducted Facebook searches on [Mother of Babies E & F] on nine separate dates between 6 August 2015 and 10 January 2016, and on [Father of Babies E & F] on one occasion. She couldn't remember making those searches and when asked for an explanation, she thought it may have been to see how [Baby F] was getting on because, as a member of staff, you'd care about what happens to the babies and obviously they had been through a really difficult time. She couldn't recall if she'd successfully accessed an account on Facebook or whether she'd found anything.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Turning to her messaging, she didn't know why she had messaged [Nurse A] at 8.53 on 5 August with [Baby F]'s sugar levels when they had finished their night shift, but thought maybe it was to update her.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She didn't know how she had obtained the reading for 8.00, but assumed it was from looking at his charts.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's the summary, my Lord, insofar as it goes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS
